newsitem.title: USA: S. Africa gold output stabilizing at 500 tons - JCI.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa gold output stabilizing at 500 tons - JCI.

text.p: The rate at which South African gold output is falling should slow significantly and stabilize around 500 tons a year in the next few years, said Bill Nairn, managing director of JCI Ltd, one of South Africa's leading gold miners.

"At this level, even making the most generous assumptions about increases in production in the other major gold producing countries, South Africa will remain the world's principal producer for many, many years to come," Nairn told the annual conference of Gold and Silver Institute.
South Africa has dominated world gold production, accounting for 32 percent of the 143,300 tons of gold it is estimated the world has ever produced.
This compares with nine percent for the U.S. and six percent for both Canada and Australia.
But South African production has fallen sharply in recent years.

In 1971, South Africa accounted for 79 percent of world gold production and the U.S. only 3.8 percent. By 1996, South Africa's share of world output had fallen to 21.2 percent, while the U.S. share had risen to 13.7 percent.
South Africa's production has fallen some 49 percent since 1970, from 976.3 tons per annum to 494.6 tons, roughly its 1956 level.
"It seems clear that South African production, having built to a peak a quarter century ago, is now in secular decline," Nairn said.
In addition, since the end of 1987, the industry has been under constant pressure to contain costs per ounce in the face of declining grades and a falling dollar gold price, he said.
"The margin between the gold price and costs has narrowed significantly over this period and it is therefore critical that efforts to contain costs be intensified," Nairn said.

Costs have escalated partly due to inflation and rising real wages and also because lower ore grades are now being mined and the mines are becoming deeper. Some South African gold is mined 3,000 to 4,000 meters below ground.
"But the Witwatersrand Basin is still the greatest unmined source of gold in the world," Nairn said. Nearly two billion ounces of gold remain in reserves or potential reserves.
Some 631 million ounces are mineable at current paylimits, while the potential resource could be 1,334 million ounces, he said.
But about 73 percent of the reserves and potential reserves are at depths below the surface of 2,000 to 4,000 meters, and a further 13 percent is at 4,000 to 5,000 meters.

"To put this in perspective, South Africa has produced about 46,709 tons or 1,450 million ounces of gold in the past 110 years, but that's only 43 percent of what we calculate God put there," Nairn said.
"Of course, getting the gold out of the ground is the issue," he said.
But a number of projects currently underway, valued at about $4 billion, suggest the outlook is positive, he said.
Three projects in particular are signficant:

- South Deep project at JCI's Western Areas mine, with a reserve of over 60 million ounces, is one of the world's largest known payable reserves in development, and will have a projected life of 65 years when fully onstream around 2000;

- Anglo American Corp's development of two major shaft systems, at depths of 3,400 to 5,000 meters, each costing over $1 billion, in the Western Ultra Deep Level lease area west of Johannesburg has estimated reserves of more than 50 million ounces at a grade of 12 grams per ton and a project life of 25 years.
- Avgold Ltd's projects in the northern Free State including their Target, Sun and Orbi ore reserves with a total resource of over 40 million ounces, entailing capital expenditure of $1.7 billion.

"These major developments -- along with the expansion of some existing mines and a number of small new ventures -- will result in a significant slowing down of the rate of decline of South African gold output," Nairn said. ((--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1640))
